526.title: The centurion's faith (Luke 7:1–10)
526.hook: a Roman officer says: just say the word
526.howItsDone: At Catholic Mass, just before communion, the congregation says a form of the centurion's words, saying they are not worthy for the Lord to enter under their roof and asking him only to say the word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a beam in the eye, a storehouse in the heart, and your line, out of the heart the mouth speaks.
screen: `OUT OF THE HEART THE MOUTH SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: A centurion was a military officer, and this one is not Jewish: an unlikely person at the center of a story about faith in a small Jewish town. In Capernaum, Luke says, his servant is dying, a servant "who was dear unto him." The first surprise: the centurion doesn't go to Jesus himself. He sends the elders of the Jewish community, and they plead his case warmly. He's worthy, they say: "For he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue." A foreign officer, and the town's elders are his advocates.
screen: `THE ELDERS: HE BUILT US A SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: So Jesus goes with them. When he's nearly at the house, the centurion sends friends with a message. In the King James words: "Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof." The elders said he's worthy. He says I'm not. A man who gives orders to soldiers, telling a traveling teacher, don't trouble yourself with me. Then he explains why Jesus needn't come at all: "say in a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man set under authority, having under me soldiers, and I say unto one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh." He knows a word from the right person is enough, no matter the distance. Luke says Jesus "marvelled at him." This time Jesus is the one amazed. He turns to the crowd: "I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel." When the friends get back to the house, the servant is well. In Luke's version, the centurion and Jesus never meet face to face; the whole story happens through messengers, and a word sent across a distance. Catholics echo the centurion at Mass: just before communion, the people say they are not worthy for the Lord to come under their roof, but ask him only to say the word. An officer's message, still spoken in churches today.
screen: `A MAN UNDER AUTHORITY: SAY THE WORD.`
then, large: `SAY IN A WORD, AND MY SERVANT SHALL BE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you can't easily reach right now, a friend in another city, someone in a hospital bed or a hard season. Find a word short enough to fit in one breath, thinking of you, I'm here, and say it slowly in your mind, as if it were already on its way. If you pray, you can echo the centurion and ask God only to say the word for them; if you don't, simply hold the word and the person together.
Centurion. An officer who says he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and trusts that one word, sent from a distance, is enough.
Your line: only say the word. A word can travel where you can't. That's day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: The widow of Nain (Luke 7:11–17)
527.hook: he sees a widow burying her only son and says: don't weep
527.howItsDone: Some churches read the widow of Nain at funerals and in times of grief, as a picture of Jesus noticing sorrow before anyone asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a centurion who said I am not worthy, and your line, only say the word.

Two crowds on one road. One is coming toward a small town called Nain: Jesus, his disciples, and a lot of people following, talking, full of the news from Capernaum. The other is coming out of the town gate. Slow. Quiet, except for the crying. A funeral. Men carry a body on an open bier, and behind them walks a woman. Luke says it in one sentence: the dead man was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." She has already buried her husband. Now her only son. And the two crowds meet at the gate.
screen: `AN ONLY SON, AND SHE A WIDOW.`

segments.voice: Some readers point out that in that world a widow with no son could be left without income or protection. If so, she is burying her child and her future on the same day. Then Luke writes: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." Nobody asks him for anything. No one sends for him, no friends lower anyone through a roof. He sees her, and that's enough. The Greek for compassion is splanchnizomai, related to a word for the inner organs; some translate it as being moved in the gut, a pull deep inside at someone else's pain. Then something unexpected at a funeral: "he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still." The whole procession stops. "And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother." That last phrase nearly repeats the words of 1 Kings about Elijah, when he raised a widow's son in Zarephath. The crowd says, "a great prophet is risen up among us," and, "God hath visited his people." This story begins not with a request or with faith, but with noticing a grieving stranger and being moved. Christian readers have seen God's own heart there: a God who sees the widow before anyone asks.
screen: then, large: `WHEN THE LORD SAW HER, HE HAD COMPASSION ON HER.`

segments.voice: Grief is often quiet: the man sitting too long in his parked car, the woman on the train staring at nothing, a voice on the phone worn thin. Bring to mind a stranger who might have been carrying something, and without needing their story, breathe in their heaviness and breathe out care toward them. If you pray, you can hold that stranger before God; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Splanchnizomai, Luke's Greek word for being moved with compassion, deep in the gut: a mother burying her only son meets Jesus at the gate, and before anyone asks, he is moved and gives her son back.
Your line: he had compassion on her. Nobody had to ask; he saw her, and that was enough. Day five hundred twenty-seven, done.

528.title: Wisdom's children (Luke 7:18–35)
528.hook: John had doubts in prison; Jesus answers with what's happening
528.carry: go and tell what you've seen
528.howItsDone: Some churches read Matthew's telling of John's question from prison during Advent, and some Christians take comfort that even John the Baptist sent his doubt to Jesus as a question.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two crowds at the gate of Nain, and your line, he had compassion on her.

John the Baptist is locked up. Luke told us earlier that Herod shut him in prison for criticizing the ruler's marriage. The man who lived in open desert air now sits in a cell. His followers bring him news: healings, crowds, a widow's son raised. News like that might encourage him. Instead, John sends two of his disciples to Jesus with a question that sounds like doubt: "Art thou he that should come? or look we for another?" This is the man who baptized Jesus, who said he wasn't worthy to untie his sandals. Even John, it seems, can wonder in the dark.

Jesus doesn't scold John for asking, and doesn't even answer yes. Luke says that in that same hour he healed many, then told the messengers: "Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached." Not an argument: a report. The list echoes the scroll of Isaiah that Jesus read in Nazareth, sight to the blind, good news to the poor, and lets John draw the line himself. Then a gentle line: "And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me." Behind offended is the Greek skandalizo, to trip up; its noun, skandalon, is a snare or stumbling block. Blessed is anyone who doesn't trip over a Messiah different from what they expected. As soon as the messengers leave, Jesus praises John: "Among those that are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist." The question hasn't lowered him. Then a picture of children in the marketplace, complaining: we played the flute and you didn't dance; we sang a sad song and you didn't cry. John came fasting, and some said he had a devil. Jesus came eating and drinking, and some called him a glutton. Nothing satisfies the critics. "But wisdom is justified of all her children." Wisdom is proved right by what she produces.
screen: `BLESSED IS HE NOT OFFENDED IN ME.`
`WE PIPED AND YE DID NOT DANCE.`
then, large: `WISDOM IS JUSTIFIED OF ALL HER CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Some questions are hard to say out loud, about faith, a relationship, a path already chosen; if you have one, name it plainly in a sentence, the way John did, without answering it. Then, instead of an argument, think about what you've actually seen and heard lately that speaks to it, either way. If you pray, you can ask your question to God plainly; if you don't, simply hold it with honesty.
Wisdom's children. John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one, and Jesus answers with what's happening, and says wisdom is proved right by her children.
Your line: go and tell what you've seen. Asking didn't make John any smaller. See you tomorrow.

529.title: She loved much (Luke 7:36–50)
529.hook: a woman with a reputation washes his feet with her tears at a proud host's dinner
529.howItsDone: Some Christians read this story when thinking about confession and forgiveness, and the woman's tears are often remembered as a picture of love and repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: John's question from prison, and your line, go and tell what you've seen.

A dinner party at the house of a Pharisee named Simon. The guests recline on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow, feet stretched out behind them. Some historians think dinners like this could be semi-public, with people from town standing at the edges to listen. One of them slips in. Luke calls her "a woman in the city, which was a sinner." He never says what her sin was, and never gives her name. She carries an alabaster jar of perfumed oil, and stands behind Jesus, at his feet. And before she can do whatever she came to do, she starts to cry.

In the King James words, she "began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment." Simon thinks, but doesn't say: if this man were a prophet, he'd know what kind of woman this is. Jesus answers the thought: "Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee." And Simon, politely: "Master, say on." Jesus speaks to him by name, as his host, not as a villain. Two people owe a moneylender, one five hundred coins, one fifty. Neither can pay, and he forgives them both. "Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?" Simon: "I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most." Then Jesus turns toward the woman, still talking to Simon: "Seest thou this woman?" Simon has seen a reputation. Jesus asks him to see a person. You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she hasn't stopped kissing my feet. You didn't anoint my head; she anointed my feet. "Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little." And to her: "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace." She came in carrying a reputation. She leaves carrying peace.
screen: then, large: `HER SINS, WHICH ARE MANY, ARE FORGIVEN; FOR SHE LOVED MUCH.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've done that still makes you wince, maybe already forgiven, by the person or by God, and never quite let in. Picture yourself at that table in the woman's place and hear the words: not it didn't matter, just forgiven, go in peace. If you pray, you can hear them as spoken to you; if you don't, simply practice setting the weight down.
Agapao, the Greek word for love behind the phrase she loved much: an unnamed woman at a Pharisee's dinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears, and leaves forgiven, in peace.
Your line: seest thou this woman. A reputation is not the whole of a person. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

530.title: The women who paid (Luke 8:1–3)
530.hook: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others funded his work
530.howItsDone: Many churches honor Mary Magdalene with a feast on July 22, and Orthodox Christians remember her among the Myrrh-bearing Women, who went to the tomb with spices.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a woman's tears at Simon's table, and your line, seest thou this woman.

Somebody has to pay for the bread. Thirteen men walking from village to village don't eat on good intentions. Someone buys the food, finds the beds, mends the sandals. Matthew and Mark never say who. Luke does, in three short verses that are easy to read straight past. Jesus went through every city and village, preaching, "and the twelve were with him." Then Luke names who else is on the road. Women, several named and many more not. And he tells us exactly what they were doing.

In the King James words: "And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance." Of their substance means out of their own money and goods. These women were funding the work. Mary, from Magdala, a fishing town on the lake, healed of seven demons. That's all Luke says about her past. Nothing about her being a prostitute; that idea came centuries later, when a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century merged her with yesterday's unnamed woman. Eastern churches never made that link, and in modern times Catholic teaching has also set it aside. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, who managed the household of Herod Antipas, the ruler who imprisoned John the Baptist. So money from inside that palace was quietly feeding Jesus' work. And Susanna, mentioned here and nowhere else in the New Testament. One verse, and she's remembered for two thousand years. The word for ministered is diakoneo, to serve, to provide, the root of the word deacon. And when the men scatter at the end of the Gospel, these women are still there. Luke names Mary Magdalene and Joanna among the women at the empty tomb, the first to hear that he is risen. The ones who paid for the road were the first witnesses at its end.
screen: `MARY MAGDALENE: SEVEN DEMONS, NOT A PAST.`
then, large: `MANY OTHERS, WHICH MINISTERED UNTO HIM OF THEIR SUBSTANCE.`

segments.voice: Think about the work you're part of, a family, a team, a church, a household, and look for the people at the edges of the picture: who keeps the calendar, pays the bill without saying so, stays late to clean up. Let one face come clearly, and picture what would fall apart if they stopped. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold them in gratitude.

Diakoneo, Greek for serving, providing for, the root of the word deacon: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others, who supported Jesus' work from their own means and were first at the empty tomb.
Your line: the women paid. Quiet support is real work, and Luke wrote their names down. That's day five hundred thirty.

531.title: An honest and good heart (Luke 8:4–21)
531.hook: the good soil keeps the word and bears fruit with patience
531.howItsDone: The parable of the sower is often read in churches and used in Christian teaching as a way to reflect on how people hear and keep scripture over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others, and your line, the women paid.

A tomato seed goes into the ground. You water it and check it the next morning. Nothing. A week later, a thin green thread. Weeks after that, maybe, something red. The waiting is the hard part. A huge crowd has gathered from town after town, and Jesus tells them a story about exactly that. "A sower went out to sow his seed." Some lands on the path, trampled and eaten by birds. Some on rock, where it sprouts and withers for lack of moisture. Some among thorns that choke it. And some on good ground, where it grows and bears a hundredfold.

Jesus explains: "The seed is the word of God." The path is people who hear, but the word is snatched away. The rock is people who receive it with joy but have no root, and fall away when testing comes. The thorns are people choked by "cares and riches and pleasures of this life." Then the good ground, with two details. In the King James words: "But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience." An honest and good heart: in Greek, kale kai agathe, a pairing some scholars say Greek writers used for a noble, upright person. And with patience: hupomone, endurance; some readers unpack it as remaining under, staying put under a weight. The good soil isn't where things happen fast. It holds on through the season. Then two short sayings. A lamp isn't lit to be put under a bed. And: "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Not just what: how. Finally, Jesus' mother and brothers arrive and can't reach him through the crowd, and he says: "My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it." Some readers take that not as pushing his family away but as widening the circle; Luke has already shown Mary keeping words in her heart. Hear and keep. Keep and do. Do, and wait.
screen: `THE SEED IS THE WORD OF GOD.`
then, large: `KEEP IT, AND BRING FORTH FRUIT WITH PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Think of something growing slowly in your life, a friendship you're rebuilding, someone else's recovery, maybe so slowly you doubt it's growing at all. Picture it as a seed in late-winter ground, where the not-seeing is part of the process; breathe in, remaining under, and breathe out the need to see results today. If you pray, you can ask for patience with slow things; if you don't, simply rest with the waiting.
Hupomone, Luke's Greek word for patience, endurance, staying under a weight: in the parable of the sower, the good soil is people who hear the word, keep it, and bear fruit with patience.
Your line: bear fruit with patience. Good soil holds on through the whole season. Day five hundred thirty-one, done.

532.title: The storm and the tombs (Luke 8:22–39)
532.hook: he stills a storm, then heals a man living among graves
532.tomorrow: your faith has made you well
532.howItsDone: Some Christians pray with the stilling of the storm in times of fear, and the healed man sent home to tell his story is sometimes read as a picture of faith shared first with family and neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sower and an honest and good heart, and your line, bear fruit with patience.

"Let us go over unto the other side of the lake." They push off, and he falls asleep in the boat. On a small boat, the mood can change in minutes. Luke says "there came down a storm of wind on the lake." Water pours in. Some of these men are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified. And the teacher is still asleep. Two stories follow, one on the water and one among graves, with a single thread: chaos, then a sudden quiet.
screen: `LET US GO OVER TO THE OTHER SIDE.`
`A STORM CAME DOWN ON THE LAKE.`

segments.voice: They wake him: "Master, master, we perish." And Luke says: "he arose, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water: and they ceased, and there was a calm." The Greek for calm is galene, the glassy stillness of the sea after the wind drops. Then a question, not a lecture: "Where is your faith?" Now they're afraid in a new way, and full of wonder: "What manner of man is this! for he commandeth even the winds and water, and they obey him." On the far shore, in the country of the Gadarenes, pigs are feeding on the hillside. A man runs out who, Luke says, "ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs." Chained and guarded, he broke free again and again. Jesus asks a plain human question: "What is thy name?" He answers: "Legion." A legion was a Roman army unit, and Luke explains: "many devils were entered into him." He doesn't have a name of his own anymore, just a crowd. Jesus frees him; the spirits go into the pigs, which rush into the lake. The townspeople find the man "sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind." The same quiet as on the lake. He begs to go with Jesus. Jesus says no: "Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee." And he goes, telling the whole city.
screen: then, large: `RETURN TO THINE OWN HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly until the water inside you is a little glassier, then think of someone in a storm right now: a friend who's panicking, a child who can't sleep. You can't command the wind, but picture yourself as the calm one in the boat, a steady voice, a slow question: what's really going on? If you pray, you can hold them before God; if you don't, simply send them stillness.
Galene, the Greek word for a calm, the glassy stillness of the sea when the wind drops: Jesus stills a storm, then frees a man among the tombs and sends him home.

Your line: return to your house. A week of a centurion, a widow, John's question, a woman's tears, the women who paid, good soil and a calm sea. Day five hundred thirty-two, and another week on the path.
